## 2026-10-15 Q0 research run (19:00 EDT) — KEVIN BACON CHAINS

### Chain 1 — the beaten type (start: B-969 "The Ink Ball", shipped 2026-10-14)
1. **B-969's ink ball → the ink ball itself.** A dabber: specially treated sheep, calf or dog leather stuffed with wool, with a wooden handle (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ink_ball). Inked in PAIRS — ink on one ball, worked together until thickness, consistency and uniformity, then the inker "beat" the type (museum examples at the Rembrandt House Museum, Amsterdam; a pair on a rack at the Bibliographical Press, Bodleian Library, Oxford). Fresh angle: the inking was always a two-handed calibration — one ball never sufficed; the pair IS the tool.
2. **The pair → the replacement.** Mid-to-late 19th century: the composition roller — glue + molasses/treacle, developed in England in the 1810s by Robert Harrild; Bryan Donkin first applied it to a machine press (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composition_roller). Leather "skin rollers" were tried and failed — the stitching seam showed on the printed type. Fresh angle: mechanization killed the pair-beat, and the labor-saving device was the key factor in the growth of mechanized presses; the seam betrays the shortcut.
3. **The labor → the devil's name for it.** Printer's devil: the ink-blackened apprentice (Collins: named for ink-covered apprentices); Titivillus — the demon originally blamed for errors in manuscripts — adapted to the new technology of printing; worn type thrown into the HELLBOX for melt-and-recast (thefreelibrary.com — early printing press depictions; lineage to the banked "The Hellbox" MEDIA SCHOOL episode and THE PRINTER'S DEVIL background figure, inventoried 12:00/14:15 runs). Fresh angle: the error itself has a named devil; the mistake is staff.
4. **The devil's apprentice → Twain.** Mark Twain started as a teenage printer's devil; Bruce Michelson's "Printer's Devil: Mark Twain and the American Publishing Revolution" argues the "radical reinvention of print" made America's first true media icon (news.illinois.edu). Fresh angle: the drudgery job was the media career's on-ramp — the devil graduates.
5. **Terminal node — THE BEAT FORM.** The type is beaten in pairs; the paired rhythm is the calibration. Ink is only right when two hands agree on it. (Banked as "The Beating"; background figure THE PRINTER'S DEVIL — job = the beating's drudgery, motive = the devil graduates.)

### Chain 2 — the unworn shoe (start: B-968 "The Glass Slipper", shipped 2026-10-14)
1. **B-968's slipper → Perrault's choice.** Charles Perrault, 1697: the slipper is glass — and deliberately so. The mishearing theory (verre "glass" for vair "squirrel fur") was put about by Honoré de Balzac; Snopes and the majority of scholars reject it — Perrault intended glass all along (365cinderellas.com; centralvetclinic.com PDF). Fresh angle: the impossible material is not an error — it is the point; the fairy tale ships an unwearable object and nobody blinks.
2. **The glass → the shoe's ancestry.** Earliest narrative: the Thracian courtesan Rhodopis marrying the King of Egypt, with a royal shoe-search; the Chinese Ye Xian; the Grimms' Aschenputtel — where the slipper is GOLD and the stepsisters cut off toe and heel to fake the fit (365cinderellas.com; anne-marie.eu). Fresh angle: the slipper's material is version-dependent (glass/gold/fur) — the fit is the fiction, not the material.
3. **The prop → the museum shoe.** Corning Museum of Glass holds a clear glass slipper made for a film version of *Cinderella* that was NEVER COMPLETED — plus a 500-pound glass coffin (the Snow White parallel) kept in the warehouse (wuot.org). Fresh angle: the prop outlives the production; the archive keeps the shoe of a film that never existed.
4. **The unworn → the unwearable.** The 2015 live-action slippers were Swarovski crystal in three separate parts — because, per costume designer Sandy Powell, glass doesn't sparkle; Lily James never wore them and CG did the walking (cinderella.fandom.com). Fresh angle: the named material fails on camera, so the real material is swapped for the effect — the honest prop is never worn.
5. **Terminal node — THE UNFINISHED SHOE.** Made to be seen, never worn; the film was never shot; glass doesn't sparkle. (Banked as "The Unworn Shoe"; background figure THE PROP KEEPER — job = the unworn shoe, motive = the film was never finished.)

### Chain 3 — the mended net (start: B-970 "The Mended Net", shipped 2026-10-14)
1. **B-970's mending → the knot grammar.** The Australian fisheries manual (P.D. Lorimer, reprinted by Oregon State): the knots are named — starting knot, right side, left side, pickup, finishing; hours spent washing natural fibres, preserving them with tar or tannin; synthetics arrived in the 1950s but nets STILL get damaged and are repaired by hand (digitalcollections.library.oregon.gov). Fresh angle: the net's vocabulary is the mending; the manual is a list of named knots.
2. **The knots → the 63-year man.** Jean Gros, Morgan City, Louisiana: 63 years making and repairing shrimp nets; hurt in 1959 off Galveston, mending full-time since 1998; repaired 38 nets the year before Katrina; nets 43 and 44 this year — "I have people come from all over that bring me their nets" (The Eunice News, 2014; archive.eunicetoday.com). Fresh angle: the trade's continuity is one man counting nets; the numbers are the institution.
3. **The continuity → the revival.** Nova Scotia: 19-year-old Garrett Henneberry fishes herring and mends — learned from father and uncle; "I want this to last for my lifetime and when I eventually have kids" (fisherynation.com). Fresh angle: the art survives by being chosen, not inherited by default — the apprentice volunteers.
4. **The trade → the prehistory.** Netting shuttles/needles trace back to the Neolithic; a red-deer-antler shuttle with stinging-nettle cordage (youtube.com — experimental archaeology). Fresh angle: the tool predates the material it works — the shuttle is older than the net.
5. **Terminal node — THE MENDED.** The net returns to the sea with its mending history in the knots; synthetic fibres didn't end the hand work. (Banked as "The Mending"; background figure THE MENDER — job = the mending, motive = the knots are the history.)

### Chain 4 — the trimmed wick (start: B-972 "The Trimmed Wick", shipped 2026-10-14)
1. **B-972's wick → the wickies.** Lighthouse keepers were nicknamed "wickies" for the job trimming the wicks — plus replenishing fuel, winding clockworks, cleaning lenses (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lighthouse_keeper). The Port Patrick keeper's 1802 instructions: trim the wicks of each oil lamp to precisely THREE-SIXTEENTHS of an inch; clean reflectors with linen or cotton rags; windows inside with rags, outside with fresh water and a mop (odysseytraveller.com). Fresh angle: the flame's survival was measured to the sixteenth — precision IS the job.
2. **The oil era → the ghost light.** Gas-lit theatres left a dim light burning to relieve pressure on the gas valves (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_light_(theatre)); the superstition layer: every theatre has a ghost, and the light either appeases the ghosts (they perform at night) or scares them off; the Palace Theatre, London keeps TWO balcony seats permanently bolted open for its ghosts. Fresh angle: the safety lamp became the ghost's stage; the held seats are the institution's permanent reservation.
3. **The ritual light → the booth cue.** The changeover cue mark: motor cue ~8s before reel end, changeover cue ~1s; each mark lasts exactly 4 frames = 0.17s = one-sixth of a second (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cue_mark; Fight Club's "cigarette burn"). Fresh angle: film exhibition's whole grammar is "catch the blink or fail" — the 8s/1s two-stage warning is a count, not a signal. NOTE: THE PROJECTION BOOTH + THE CHANGEOVER CUE + the banked [READY] "The Changeover" episode and [DRAFT] "The Changeover" venture already own this angle — this chain's terminal node leans on the wick/trim + held-seats side instead (lineage flagged).
